public_rationale: The evidence supports substantial parts of the warning. OpenAI acknowledged factual unreliability, NewsGuard repeatedly elicited false claims, and March testing found suicide-risk judgments below professional norms. But leading prompts do not establish how often ordinary answers were false, and a narrow suicide-risk study cannot establish reliability across mental-health and marriage advice. Favorable case findings also show that helpful responses were possible, without proving dependable safety. The full compound claim remains unresolved.
limitations: Most decisive evidence concerns ChatGPT rather than a representative sample of chatbots.
The reporting period and ordinary meaning of constantly require interpretation.
Supporting evidence for several components does not settle the unmeasured components.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Current chatbots constantly produce misinformation and cannot be trusted to answer real-world questions or give sound mental-health or marriage advice.

statement.excerpt: Yes, they can generate cool haikus and well-written prose, but they also constantly spew misinformation (even about themselves), and cannot be trusted when it comes to answering questions about real-world events and phenomena, let alone to provide sound advice about mental health or marriage counseling.
statement.document_title: Stop Treating AI Models Like People

from_speaker: answering questions about real-world events and phenomena
sound advice about mental health or marriage counseling
our_interpretation: The claim concerns general-purpose conversational language models available when the post appeared, not later systems or purpose-built clinical tools.
The ordinary reading is that material falsehoods recur and answers require independent checking, especially for consequential advice. It does not mean every answer is false.
Because the ongoing observation names no reporting period, I use January–March 2023, the latest completed calendar quarter before publication.
The full claim includes factual reliability, mental-health advice, and marriage counseling. Evidence for one component does not automatically establish the others.
criteria.support_condition: Period-matched evaluations show recurring material factual errors in ordinary question answering, together with expert assessments showing that mental-health and marriage advice cannot reliably be followed without independent checks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Broad, representative evaluations of the same systems show dependable factual answers and sound advice in the named settings, with errors sufficiently rare and well signaled to undermine the claim of recurring unreliability. Selected correct answers alone would not suffice.

evidence.locator: Opening results discussion, paragraph beginning In January 2023
evidence.explanation: The test demonstrates repeated misinformation generation under leading prompts. Because researchers sought false narratives and counted responses containing later disclaimers, this is not an ordinary-use factual-error rate.

evidence.locator: Abstract; testing dates in Methods, Artificial intelligence procedure
evidence.explanation: Tests conducted March 20–30 found consistently lower suicide-risk assessments than professional norms, supporting concern about consequential mental-health judgments. This narrow vignette comparison does not measure counseling outcomes or marriage advice.

evidence.locator: Section ChatGPT for patients in psychotherapeutic treatment
evidence.explanation: The expert case analysis found useful responses while warning against replacing psychotherapy. It qualifies an interpretation that no helpful advice was possible, but April conversations and limited cases prevent it from settling reliability during the target quarter.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Representative evaluations of contemporaneous chatbot outputs, with ordinary factual questions and expert-rated mental-health and marriage advice, would establish whether material failures recurred broadly enough to justify the claim.
